newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aussie dlr depressed as wages add to rate pressure.
newsitem.headline: Aussie dlr depressed as wages add to rate pressure.

text.p: The Australian dollar extended an early slide at the midsession after weak wages data piled pressure on the Reserve Bank to cut rates for a fifth time.

The figures showed average weekly ordinary time earnings rose a modest 0.5 percent in the May quarter dragging annual growth down to 3.7 percent from 4.3 in Q1, the lowest rise in almost three years. Forecasts had favoured gains of 0.8 percent and 4.1 percent respectively.
The subdued result confirmed the historically low inflation enviroment seen in the Q2 consumer price data was here to stay and had the money market clamouring for a cut in official rates.

By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the dollar was on the defensive at US$0.7339/44 having briefly dipped as deep as US$0.7327 immediately after the data from an early US$0.7363/68 and US$0.7373/78 late here Wednesday.
Traders said there were good bids beneath US$0.7330 and strong chart support around US$0.7310 which marked an 18-month low from last week.

Many thought the dollar had held up well given the message from all the inflation data was that the RBA could safely cut at any time. The resilience of support suggested an easing could already be priced into the A$ after weeks of steady decline.
Whether the support would last if and when the easing became reality and Australian official rates moved below those in the U.S. was harder to say, although many were quietly bullish.
Analysts could see no reason why the RBA should not cut as soon as Friday morning although some reckoned it would wait for its next board meeting on August 5.

Most still looked for a 0.50 point easing to 5.00 percent but noted the inflation outlook was so benign the bank could well cut by 75 basis points. Such a move would bring rates back to where they were before the last tightening phase started in August 1994 and perhaps stop consumers from waiting for more.
Economists suspect consumers may have been delaying spending decisions in the expectation of further cuts and if the bank eased by just 0.50 point they would simply wait for another.

Analysts noted the AWOTE rise of 3.7 percent was well below the 4.5 percent danger line which the RBA regarded as a threat to inflation and would come as a huge relief to the bank which had long been frustrated by the stubborness of wage growth.

The weak wages data argued for a cut in a second way in that it implied the earnings, salaries and supplements contribution to GDP growth would be low in the June quarter -- if pay rises were lower then people did not have so much to spend.
The futures market certainly saw the figures as a green light and chased the September 90-day bank bill contract eight basis points higher to 94.97, implying a rate of 5.03 percent.

The comparable Eurodollar future was at 94.275 reflecting the risk the Federal Reserve may hike the 5.50 percent funds sometime down the track, so the A$ already effectively yielded around 75 basis points less than the US$.

This was a new, and not entirely welcome, experience for a market used to thinking of the A$ as a high yielder and dealers suspected it would take time for it to accept that Australian fundamentals were so good the A$ did not need a risk premium.

The process had already gone a long way in the bond market where the yield spread on local and U.S. 10-year bonds had narrowed from over 200 basis points in the last couple of years to just 25 today, the lowest level since financial markets were deregulated in the early 1980s.
The growing offshore confidence in Australia this narrowing reflected should be supportive of the dollar in the longer term and perhaps limit the shockwave should the RBA finally ease.
On the crosses the dollar was steady at 84.92/02 yen from 84.95/05 Wednesday but down at 57.0 in trade weighted terms from 57.2. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
